And this next report provides some insight into the status of the city's primary water mains and water distribution system.
The recent large scale water main breaks in the cities of Calgary and Montreal have raised public awareness of the risk that large municipalities face with respect to water services.
Understandably residents have questions about the reliability and resiliency of the city's critical water distribution infrastructure.

This information report provides insight on the state of our water infrastructure and the various asset management initiatives we have in place to minimize risks of water main breaks and the impacts when they do occur.
The greatest risk to service interruption lies in more than one film main or primary water main failing at the same time.
Since 2007, the city has experienced on average just under eight primary water main or filming breaks per year with a low of three in each of 2017, 2018 and 2019 and a high of 23 breaks in 2008.
This is trending downwards and during these breaks and plan shutdowns for maintenance, no city wide water restrictions have been required.
Preservation of the water main of the primary water main and filming network is funded through the water utility and infrastructure level and the long term strategy.
Include funding requirements and funding gaps are identified in the water distribution asset management plan which is updated every two years as part of the multi year budget approval cycle.
In 2015, the city undertook a pipeline risk prioritization study. This study assigned a risk score to every primary water main by evaluating the likelihood and consequence of a failure.
Pice with high risk scores were prioritized for further inspection.

Inspections of primary water mains occur on a regular basis and if concerns are identified, repair and rehabilitation is planned and completed similar to what is occurring on college drive this summer.
In addition, the city is developing a critical spirit strategy to minimize the risk of disruptions due to supply chain delays.

The information report provides a lot more detail on the specific asset management initiatives that are currently underway to ensure the reliability and resiliency of Saskatoon's water distribution system.

A feature long-term plan and funding strategy for recommended inspections and preservation will be included in the next water distribution asset management plan which will be presented in 2025 prior to the next budget deliberations.

At the City Council meeting in June, Councillor DeWatt made an inquiry requesting a report back to outline a review process and resources needed to undertake a pilot project.
For the conversion of the Eastview neighborhood from rear lane to front street solid waste recycling and organics cart collection.
Just to provide some history on this, in 2002 the City began conversion of large communal garbage bins in mirror lanes to individual bins collected on the front street.
This was done for several reasons to support waste management efforts, as well as to reduce damage to rear lanes and collection trucks and to limit opportunities for vandalism and litter.
Ultimately, the decision to convert a neighborhood was based on feedback from residents and consultation with the councillor in the area.

Today approximately 25% of residential properties continue to have waste collection in the rear lane and we have committed to undertaking a review in 2025 to determine the appropriate location for collections.

To address this inquiry, the administration has developed a review process which includes engagement with impacted residents that could be used as a pilot in Eastview prior to undertaking a full review of the outstanding location.
The proposed engagement plan is outlined in the report and includes a flyer mail-out advising of the proposed changes and dates for engagement activities.
A city of Saskatoon engagement website that includes a survey as well as a virtual question and answer sessions for residents.
The goal of the engagement would be to share information with residents and provide city staff with insight into preferences and highlight any unintended consequences of the proposed changes.

If the results of the engagement activities indicated that there is a clear preference for the Eastview neighborhood to convert to front street collections, then the decision would need or would be made to do so in consultation with the councillor of the area.
The cost for this engagement in Eastview is estimated at $8,000 and could be completed within the current operating program.

Great. Thank you again Madam Chair. The city of Saskatoon currently operates curbside and multi unit single stream recycling programs and participates in the public.
And participates in the provincial multi material stewardship western program or NNSW for short.
Where the city receives funding based on the number of households to support recycling and waste diversion programs.

In 2023, the Saskatchewan Ministry of Environment released the household packaging and paper stewardship program regulations that shifts the responsibility of providing recycling services to producers.
Where producers would assume full operational and financial responsibility in managing household packaging and paper.
As such, NNSW has drafted a stewardship plan that has been approved by the Ministry of Environment to fulfill the requirements of the new regulations.
With the new provincial regulations and plans in place, changes to NNSW funding will be occurring.
Saskatoon will essentially have three options to choose from going forward.

The first option is a community-led collection model. In this model, municipalities would be contracted by NNSW to provide curbside and multi-family collection and deliver the materials to NNSW recycling facility for processing.

A master service agreement and statement of work would outline the city's responsibilities for collections, containers, customer service, education and performance targets for capture and contamination rates of the materials.
The second option is a program-led collection model, which would essentially remove the city from the majority of the process.
NNSW would provide the collections services as well as the processing and as mentioned, the city would have little involvement in the recycling programs.

Under both of these options NNSW would set service levels and be responsible for establishing the types of acceptable materials for recycling. However, at this time, we don't anticipate a significant change to the current city's current service levels based on our discussions with NNSW.
There is a third option, and will not an official option, the city could maintain status quo until December 1, 2027 at which time the current funding model will cease.

Over the coming months, the administration will complete an analysis of these options that will include financial implications, environmental outcomes, reviewing feedback from previous resident program satisfaction results and finding from discussions with other jurisdictions participating in similar programs in British Columbia.
The preliminary analysis of the options noted above has identified that each option will have unique financial implications that will be presented when the future decision is made.
We will be bringing back a recommendation for Council's consideration in early 2025 to meet the timeline of March 1, 2025.
So with that, it's an information report for committee's consideration this morning, and we're available if there's any questions.
